analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicaid to cover doula and midwife care during pregnancy, birth, and postpartum.
analysis.headline: The Mamas First Act was referred to a House committee and its Health subcommittee in April 2022, received no hearing or vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have added doula and midwife services to the list of care every state Medicaid program must cover, including prenatal, delivery, and postpartum support, in homes, birth centers, hospitals, clinics, or by telehealth [S3]. Medicaid pays for roughly four in ten births in the United States, so the bill would primarily reach low-income pregnant women, with the bill text citing CDC data showing maternal deaths among Black women (43.5 per 100,000 births) run more than three times the rate for white women (12.7) [S3]. It never advanced past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income pregnant women on Medicaid, who would gain guaranteed coverage for non-medical labor support (doulas) and midwife-led birth care; the bill text cites NIH findings that doula-assisted mothers are four times less likely to have a low-birth-weight baby [S3]. Doulas and midwives would gain a large new paying client base, since states could no longer treat their services as optional [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Pregnant Medicaid recipients; doulas and midwives

how_it_helps.text: Makes doula and midwife care a mandatory Medicaid benefit covering prenatal, delivery, and postpartum care, in the home, community, hospital, birth center, clinic, health unit, or via telehealth where state law allows [S3].

Adds tribal midwives recognized by Indian tribes to the covered provider definition, addressing the CDC maternal mortality rate of 32.5 per 100,000 births for American Indian and Alaska Native women cited in the bill [S3].

The bill's findings cite NIH evidence that doula-assisted mothers are four times less likely to have a low-birth-weight baby and twice as likely to initiate breastfeeding, and that midwife-led care is associated with lower cesarean and preterm birth rates [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government and state Medicaid programs would bear the cost of covering these new mandatory services; states also face a new federal mandate that some would need legislation to implement, for which the bill allows a delayed compliance period [S3]. Hospital maternity services could see some Medicaid revenue shift toward lower-intervention midwife-led and doula-supported births [S3].

drawbacks.text: Adding a mandatory benefit means new federal and state Medicaid spending at a time when states must balance their budgets, and the mandate would require some state legislatures to act before their programs could comply [S3].

The bill's definition of a doula requires 60 hours of foundational training plus certification from an organization established for at least five years with continuing education, which could exclude experienced community doulas who lack formal certification [S3].

The midwife definition requires meeting the International Confederation of Midwives global standards, a bar stricter than the licensure some U.S. states use for community midwives, which could exclude some currently practicing midwives [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and targeted: guaranteed doula and midwife coverage for Medicaid births, in a country whose maternal mortality rate the bill calls the highest in the developed world, with deaths falling hardest on Black and Indigenous women [S3]. The main cost is Medicaid spending, though the bill's own findings argue midwife-led care is associated with cost savings through fewer cesareans and preterm births [S3]. The training and certification thresholds are tighter than many advocates would prefer and risk screening out existing community doulas [S3]. On balance the bill aimed a concrete benefit at a well-documented crisis, and its main design question is whether the certification requirements are too restrictive.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health subcommittee on April 7-8, 2022, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Gwen Moore (D-WI) introduced the Mamas First Act on April 7, 2022, with four Democratic cosponsors: Reps. Underwood, Adams, Dingell, and Pressley [S1][S3][S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on April 7, 2022, and to that committee's Subcommittee on Health on April 8, 2022 [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospital-based maternity care providers keep their current Medicaid revenue uninterrupted, and federal and state budgets are spared the new mandatory benefit. The women the bill was written for, particularly Black and Indigenous Medicaid recipients, gained nothing because the maternal mortality rates the bill cited are unchanged [S3].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospital maternity care and existing budgets

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require Medicaid coverage of doula and midwife services

for.name: Reps. Underwood, Adams, Dingell, and Pressley

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee

against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup; it died there when the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: All five House supporters were Democrats, but no committee hearing or vote ever occurred, so no one was recorded opposing the bill on its merits.

industries.note: The bill would have made their services a mandatory Medicaid benefit, creating a large new paying patient base. Their interest runs alongside patients': more covered births attended by doulas and midwives.

industries.industry: Hospital maternity care and obstetric physician practices
industries.note: Some Medicaid spending could shift toward midwife-led, lower-intervention births, which the bill's own findings link to fewer cesareans and cost savings. Hospital and physician billing for higher-intervention deliveries would face new competition.

The bill requires doulas to be certified by an organization established for at least five years with continuing education requirements, making those certifying bodies the gatekeepers to Medicaid payment and potentially excluding doulas without such credentials.
